claim: Six of the ten most populated folds in the Structural Classification of Proteins (SCOP) have repetitive structures.
source: six of the ten most populated folds in the Structural Classification of Proteins (SCOP) (Murzin et al., 1995) – including the five most frequent ones – have repetitive structures.
evidence: The manuscript cites SCOP database (Murzin et al., 1995) as the source for this structural classification data.

claim: The tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) was originally identified as a repeating 34 amino-acid motif in Cdc23p of Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: This was originally identified as a repeating 34 amino-acid motif in Cdc23p of Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Sikorski et al., 1990) – hence its name.
evidence: The manuscript cites Sikorski et al., 1990 as the original identification of TPR.

claim: TPR-containing proteins have been discovered in all kingdoms of life.
source: Since then, TPR-containing proteins have been discovered in all kingdoms of life, where they mediate protein-protein interactions in a broad range of biological processes, such as cell cycle control, transcription, protein translocation, protein folding, signal transduction and innate immunity (Cortajarena and Regan, 2006; Dunin-Horkawicz et al., 2014; Katibah et al., 2014; Keiski et al., 2010; Kyrpides and Woese, 1998; Lamb et al., 1995; Sikorski et al., 1990).
evidence: Multiple citations support the widespread distribution and functional diversity of TPR proteins.

claim: The first crystal structure of a TPR domain showed that the repeat units are helical hairpins, stacked into a continuous, right-handed superhelical architecture.
source: The ﬁrst crystal structure of a TPR domain (Das et al., 1998) showed that the repeat units are helical hairpins, stacked into a continuous, right-handed superhelical architecture with an inner groove that mediates the interaction with target proteins (Forrer et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites Das et al., 1998 for the first crystal structure determination.

claim: The helical hairpins in TPR proteins interact via a specific geometry involving knobs-into-holes packing and bury about 40% of their surface between repeat units.
source: The hairpins interact via a specific geometry involving knobs-into-holes packing (Crick, 1953) and burying about 40% of their surface between repeat units.
evidence: The manuscript cites Crick, 1953 for the knobs-into-holes packing concept and provides a specific quantitative measure (40% surface burial).

claim: Almost all known TPR-containing proteins can be detected using a single sequence profile.
source: Nevertheless, almost all known TPR-containing proteins can be detected using a single sequence proﬁle (Karpenahalli et al., 2007), underscoring their homologous origin.
evidence: The manuscript cites Karpenahalli et al., 2007 for the sequence profile detection method.

claim: TPR proteins generally contain at least two unit hairpins in a repeated fashion.
source: As their name implies, TPR proteins generally contain at least two unit hairpins in a repeated fashion.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation about TPR protein structure.

claim: The mitochondrial import protein Tom20 has only one TPR hairpin and is not ancestral based on its phylogenetic distribution and functionality.
source: The few that have only one hairpin, notably the mitochondrial import protein Tom20 (Abe et al., 2000), are clearly not ancestral based on their phylogenetic distribution and functionality, implying that the ancestor of the superfamily already had a repeated structure.
evidence: The manuscript cites Abe et al., 2000 and provides inference about ancestral state based on phylogenetic distribution.

claim: Ribosomal proteins most likely constitute some of the oldest proteins observable today.
source: Ribosomal proteins most likely constitute some of the oldest proteins observable today and are still intimately involved in an RNA-driven process: translation (Fox, 2010; Hsiao et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites Fox, 2010 and Hsiao et al., 2009 to support the ancient nature of ribosomal proteins.

claim: Ribosomal proteins are mostly incapable of assuming their folds outside the ribosomal context.
source: They are mostly incapable of assuming their folds outside the ribosomal context (Peng et al., 2014) and thus belong to a class of intrinsically disordered proteins that become structured upon binding to a macromolecular scaffold (Dyson and Wright, 2005; Habchi et al., 2014; Oldfield and Dunker, 2014; Peng et al., 2014; Varadi et al., 2014).
evidence: Multiple citations support the intrinsically disordered nature of ribosomal proteins outside their native context.

claim: In recently amplified TPR proteins, repeats frequently have >80% pairwise sequence identity.
source: In recently amplified proteins, such as the ones shown in Figure 1a, within which repeats frequently have >80% pairwise sequence identity, tracking the probable α-hairpin at the root of the amplification is a fairly straightforward proposition.
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific quantitative threshold (>80% identity) and references Figure 1a showing examples.

claim: TPRpred was used to scan protein sequences in the PDB for peptides that share statistically significant similarity to the TPR sequence profile using a p-value cutoff of 1.0e−4.
source: Here, in a first step, we used TPRpred to scan protein sequences in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) (Berman et al., 2000) for peptides that share statistically significant similarity to the TPR sequence profile and yet have not been annotated as TPR in Pfam (Finn et al., 2014); we used a p-value cutoff = 1.0e−4, which leads to an estimated false discovery rate of 1.0%, see Materials and methods.
evidence: The manuscript describes the computational method used with specific parameters and estimated false discovery rate.

claim: The search for TPR-like helical hairpins in non-repetitive proteins yielded 31 helical hairpins similar to the TPR unit with respect to both sequence and structure.
source: This yielded 31 helical hairpins that are similar to the TPR unit with respect to both sequence and structure.
evidence: The manuscript reports the specific number of hits from the computational search.

claim: Among the 31 helical hairpins found, 22 are part of solenoid-like structures and were discarded.
source: Among them, 22 are part of solenoid-like structures and were discarded.
evidence: The manuscript describes the filtering process and the number of hits excluded.

claim: The remaining nine hits from the TPR-like hairpin search belong to three families: mitochondrial import receptor subunit Tom20, microtubule interacting and transport (MIT) domain including katanin, and 30S ribosomal protein S20 (RPS20).
source: The remaining nine hits belong to three families: (I) mitochondrial import receptor subunit Tom20; (II) microtubule interacting and transport (MIT) domain including katanin (Iwaya et al., 2010); and (III) 30S ribosomal protein S20 (RPS20) (Figure 2).
evidence: The manuscript lists the three protein families and references Figure 2 showing their structures.

claim: The similarity of Tom20 and MIT domains to TPR proteins has been noted before.
source: The similarity of Tom20 and MIT domains to TPR proteins has been noted before (Abe et al., 2000; Iwaya et al., 2010; Scott et al., 2005), but the similarity of RPS20 was surprising and drew our attention particularly due to the ancestrality attributed to ribosomal proteins.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies that noted these similarities.

claim: The top-scoring RPS20 hit from TPRpred was RPS20-hh from Thermus aquaticus, which matches the TPR unit sequence profile at a p-value of 5.4e−07.
source: The top-scoring hit was RPS20-hh from Thermus aquaticus (NCBI accession number = WP_003044315.1, UniProt id = B7A5L8_THEAQ), which matches the TPR unit sequence proﬁle at a p-value of 5.4e−07, almost an order of magnitude better than the second hit (see Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific p-value from computational analysis.

claim: 42 RPS20-hhs were found that contain at least three hydrophobic residues out of five interface positions.
source: We found 42 RPS20-hhs that contain at least three hydrophobic residues out of the five interface positions.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of sequences meeting specific criteria from sequence analysis.

claim: Among RPS20-hhs with at least three hydrophobic interface residues, the only one predicted to match the TPR unit profile above a p-value of 1.0e−4 was RPS20 from T. aquaticus.
source: Among them, the only RPS20-hh predicted to match the TPR unit proﬁle above a p-value of 1.0e−4 was again the RPS20 from T. aquaticus, in which three of the ﬁve interface residues are hydrophobic (L10, I21 and V28).
evidence: The manuscript reports the result of computational screening with specific criteria.

claim: Three-repeat TPRs represent the most common form of this fold.
source: We focused on the construction of three-repeat TPRs, which represent the most common form of this fold (D'Andrea and Regan, 2003; Sawyer et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites two studies supporting this structural observation.

claim: 18 of the 54 non-identical TPR domains in the extended Structural Classification of Proteins database (SCOPe v2.05) have three repeats.
source: For instance, 18 of the 54 non-identical TPR domains in the extended Structural Classification of Proteins database (SCOPe v2.05) (Fox et al., 2014) have three repeats.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts from the SCOPe database.

claim: CTPR3, a previously designed three-repeat TPR protein, was demonstrated to be highly stable, even more so than natural three-repeat TPR proteins.
source: A previously designed three-repeat TPR protein, CTPR3, was also demonstrated to be highly stable, even more so than natural three-repeat TPR proteins (Main et al., 2003b).
evidence: The manuscript cites Main et al., 2003b for the stability characterization of CTPR3.

claim: The construct M0, containing no mutations, was soluble but remained unfolded under all conditions tested.
source: When we experimentally made a construct containing no mutations (M0, Table 1), it was soluble but remained unfolded under all conditions tested (see Section 2.4).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for the M0 construct.

claim: Four different sites of mutation (L4W, K7L/R, V9N, I23D/Y) were considered to improve interface hydrophobicity or preserve coevolved positions observed in TPRs.
source: Following these principles, four different sites of mutation (L4W, K7L/R, V9N, I23D/Y, see Figure 4) were considered to improve interface hydrophobicity or preserve coevolved positions observed in TPRs (Sawyer et al., 2013) (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript describes the design rationale with citation and reference to Figure 4.

claim: Natural TPR proteins tend to exhibit zero net charge.
source: Furthermore, as natural TPR proteins tend to exhibit zero net charge (Magliery and Regan, 2004), four positively charged residues were also targeted (K2E, K6N, K22E, R25Q/E, see Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript cites Magliery and Regan, 2004 for this observation about TPR protein charge.

claim: Three proteins (M0, M4RD and M5) could be purified from soluble extracts.
source: Three proteins (M0, M4RD and M5) could be purified from soluble extracts; the other constructs were insoluble and were refolded from inclusion bodies.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from protein expression and purification.

claim: In far UV circular dichroism (CD) spectra, all proteins displayed a strong alpha-helical pattern, except M0 and M4RD, which appeared to be unfolded.
source: In far UV circular dichroism (CD) spectra, all proteins displayed a strong alpha-helical pattern, except M0 and M4RD, which appeared to be unfolded, but not prone to aggregation and precipitation, even at high concentrations.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental CD spectroscopy results.

claim: M4N showed cooperative unfolding with a Tm of 77°C.
source: When we studied the melting curves, M4N showed cooperative unfolding with a Tm of 77°C (Supplementary file 1F), while the unfolding of M2, M4E and M5 did not conform to a classical two-state transition, consistent with an unstable molten globule-like state.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental thermal denaturation results.

claim: M2, M4E, M4N and M5 yielded typical cooperative denaturation curves in urea-induced unfolding transitions monitored by CD.
source: To clarify this point, urea-induced unfolding transitions were monitored by CD. Like M4N, the three variants M2, M4E and M5 yielded typical cooperative denaturation curves, indicative of folded polypeptides (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental urea denaturation results and references a figure showing the data.

claim: M5 had a λmax of 336 nm in fluorescence emission spectra, as expected for partially shielded aromatic residues.
source: In line with these findings, M5, the only protein containing tryptophan residues, had a λmax of 336 nm in fluorescence emission spectra, as expected for partially shielded aromatic residues.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental fluorescence spectroscopy results.

claim: Four of the five designed TPR variants (M2, M4E, M4N and M5) result in well-folded repeat proteins.
source: We conclude that four of the five designed TPR variants, M2, M4E, M4N and M5, result in well-folded repeat proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental characterizations (CD, urea denaturation, fluorescence).

claim: All four folded constructs (M2, M4E, M4N and M5) were exclusively dimers in static light scattering experiments.
source: To determine the oligomeric state of our folded proteins, we performed static light scattering experiments. Surprisingly, all four constructs were exclusively dimers (Supplementary file 1F).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental static light scattering results.

claim: Isolated RPS20 exhibits only one third helical content by CD.
source: It had been shown previously that isolated RPS20 exhibits only one third helical content by CD (Paterakis et al., 1983).
evidence: The manuscript cites Paterakis et al., 1983 for this previous experimental observation.

claim: RPS20 from T. aquaticus and T. thermophilus were insoluble upon expression and had to be refolded.
source: We cloned RPS20 from T. aquaticus and its close relative T. thermophilus. Upon expression, both proteins were insoluble and had to be refolded.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from protein expression.

claim: Both T. aquaticus and T. thermophilus RPS20 proteins behaved as monomers in static light scattering measurements.
source: In static light scattering measurements, both proteins behaved as monomers (Supplementary file 1F).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental static light scattering results.

claim: RPS20 exhibits considerable conformational variation in solution based on CD spectra and the absence of defined melting and urea-denaturation curves.
source: Based on CD spectra, which showed a high proportion of random structure, and the absence of defined melting and urea-denaturation curves (Supplementary file 1F), we conclude that RPS20 indeed exhibits considerable conformational variation in solution.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental characterizations.

claim: The structure of M4N was solved to a resolution of 2.2 Å.
source: We obtained crystals and solved the structure of M4N to a resolution of 2.2 Å (Figure 5a).
evidence: The manuscript reports the crystal structure determination with specific resolution.

claim: The asymmetric unit of M4N contains three polypeptide chains of almost identical structure with all pairwise Cα RMSD values below 1.4 Å.
source: The asymmetric unit (ASU) contains three polypeptide chains of almost identical structure (all pairwise Cα RMSD values below 1.4 Å).
evidence: The manuscript reports structural analysis results with specific RMSD values.

claim: All three chains in the M4N structure exhibit the desired TPR architecture with three repetitive hairpins, which interact via knobs-into-holes packing between helices.
source: Notably, all three chains exhibit the desired TPR architecture with three repetitive hairpins, which interact via knobs-into-holes packing between helices Ai and B(i-1), as is characteristic of TPR hairpins.
evidence: The manuscript reports structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: A superposition of M4N to the CTPR3 structure yields Cα RMSD values below 2.6 Å.
source: A superposition to the CTPR3 structure yields Cα RMSD values below 2.6 Å (supplementary file 1I).
evidence: The manuscript reports structural comparison results with specific RMSD values.

claim: The stop helix of M4N is not resolved in any of the three chains in the crystal structure.
source: An unexpected difference to the canonical TPR structure is that the stop helix of M4N is not resolved in any of the three chains.
evidence: The manuscript reports an observation from the crystal structure.

claim: In the M4N structure, the C-terminal TPR units of two protomers form a tight interface where the B3 helix of each chain substitutes for the stop helix of the other.
source: However, this missing helix is compensated for by a specific dimerization mode of two M4N protomers. Therein, the C-terminal TPR units of the two protomers form a tight interface, in which the B3 helix of each chain substitutes for the stop helix of the other, mimicking the capping effect of the stop helix (Figure 6).
evidence: The manuscript reports structural analysis of the crystal structure and references Figure 6.

claim: A superposition of the M4N dimer interface to the last TPR unit and stop helix of CTPR3 yields Cα RMSD values as low as 1.2 Å over 44 residues.
source: A superposition of this mimicry to the last TPR unit and stop helix of CTPR3 yields Cα RMSD values as low as 1.2 Å over 44 residues.
evidence: The manuscript reports structural comparison results with specific RMSD values.

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis revealed that the M4N stop helix had been partially proteolyzed upon expression of the protein.
source: Analysis by mass spectrometry revealed that the M4N stop helix had been partially proteolyzed upon expression of the protein (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental mass spectrometry results.

claim: Extending the stop helix with a C-terminal His6-tag (M4N-His) prevented proteolysis but did not affect stability or dimerization.
source: Extending the stop helix with a C-terminal His6-tag prevented proteolysis, but did not affect stability or dimerization (M4N-His; Supplementary file 1F).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results comparing M4N and M4N-His.

claim: An M4NΔC construct, which terminates with the B3 helix, showed the same stability and dimerization as M4N.
source: Indeed, an M4NΔC construct, which terminates with the B3 helix, showed the same stability and dimerization as M4N.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results comparing M4N and M4NΔC.

claim: Two structures for M4NΔC were obtained from different crystal forms at 2.0 Å and 1.7 Å resolution.
source: We obtained two structures for M4NΔC from different crystal forms at 2.0 Å and 1.7 Å resolution, respectively, the first (CF I) with two dimers in the ASU and the second (CF II) with a single chain in the ASU, for which we constructed the dimer by crystallographic symmetry.
evidence: The manuscript reports crystal structure determination with specific resolutions.

claim: All three M4NΔC dimers superimpose to the M4N dimer with Cα RMSD below 1.9 Å.
source: All three dimers superimpose to the M4N dimer with Cα RMSD below 1.9 Å (Figure 7, Supplementary file 1I).
evidence: The manuscript reports structural comparison results with specific RMSD values.

claim: The stop helix is dispensable for folding, dimerization and the stability of the designed constructs.
source: We conclude that the stop helix is dispensable for folding, dimerization and the stability of our designed constructs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental comparisons of M4N, M4N-His, and M4NΔC.

claim: The geometry of dimerization in M4N has not been observed in TPR structures before.
source: The geometry of dimerization in M4N has not been observed in TPR structures before.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to existing structural knowledge.

claim: Each mutation in M2 and M4N occurs in natural RPS20 sequences.
source: Each mutation in M2 and M4N occurs in natural RPS20 sequences (see Supplementary file 1A), but no RPS20 sequence has all four mutations simultaneously and we therefore tested if they can be tolerated in vivo.
evidence: The manuscript reports sequence analysis results from natural RPS20 sequences.

claim: The RPS20 helical hairpins in T. aquaticus and T. thermophilus differ only at four positions, of which two are highly conservative substitutions.
source: The RPS20 helical hairpins in T. aquaticus and T. thermophilus differ only at four positions, of which two are highly conservative substitutions (Figure 8a).
evidence: The manuscript reports sequence comparison results and references Figure 8a.

claim: Under selection pressure from kanamycin, only the 1500 bp PCR product was obtained in all cases where plasmid-borne rpsT was introduced, showing that the chromosomal gene had been fully substituted.
source: Under selection pressure from kanamycin, only the 1500 bp product was obtained in all cases where plasmid-borne rpsT was introduced, whether in wild-type or mutated form (Figure 8c panels 1 and 2, lanes TT, TA, TA2 and TA4), showing that the chromosomal gene had been fully substituted.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental PCR screening results and references Figure 8c.

claim: PCR screening of strain KM4 complemented with an empty plasmid produced both 800 bp and 1500 bp fragments.
source: In contrast, PCR screening of strain KM4 complemented with an empty plasmid produced both 800 bp and 1500 bp fragments (Figure 8c panels 1 and 2, lane E).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental PCR screening results and references Figure 8c.

claim: T. thermophilus HB8 is a polyploid organism (minimally tetraploid).
source: Since T. thermophilus HB8 is a polyploid organism (minimally tetraploid [Ohtani et al., 2010]), this result shows that rpsT can be reduced in copy number, but not fully eliminated, suggesting that the gene is essential.
evidence: The manuscript cites Ohtani et al., 2010 for the ploidy of T. thermophilus HB8.

claim: rpsT can be reduced in copy number but not fully eliminated in T. thermophilus HB8, suggesting that the gene is essential.
source: Since T. thermophilus HB8 is a polyploid organism (minimally tetraploid [Ohtani et al., 2010]), this result shows that rpsT can be reduced in copy number, but not fully eliminated, suggesting that the gene is essential.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the PCR screening results in the polyploid organism.

claim: At increased kanamycin concentration, no PCR product for chromosomal rpsT was obtained for any rpsT allele (TT, TA, TA2 and TA4).
source: At low kanamycin concentrations this protocol always generated a product (Figure 8d panel 1), but at increased kanamycin concentration we did not obtain product for any rpsT allele (Figure 8d panel 2, lanes TT, TA, TA2 and TA4).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental PCR screening results and references Figure 8d.

claim: Plasmid-borne rpsT and its mutants were able to complement the chromosomal rpsT and the latter was displaced from the population to a level that left it undetectable by PCR.
source: This demonstrates that plasmid-borne rpsT and its mutants were able to complement the chromosomal rpsT and that the latter was displaced from the population to a level that left it undetectable by PCR.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PCR screening results at different kanamycin concentrations.

claim: Chromosomal rpsT could never be completely suppressed in strain KM4 complemented with an empty plasmid, even under high kanamycin conditions (120 µg/ml).
source: In contrast, we could never completely suppress chromosomal rpsT in strain KM4 complemented with an empty plasmid, even under high kanamycin conditions (120 µg/ml).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from PCR screening under high selection pressure.

claim: rpsT is essential in T. thermophilus.
source: We found that rpsT is essential in T. thermophilus, but that its loss could be complemented by wild-type and mutant T. aquaticus rpsT, and that this complementation restored wild-type levels of growth (Figure 8e).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the inability to completely eliminate rpsT and the complementation experiments.

claim: The loss of rpsT in T. thermophilus could be complemented by wild-type and mutant T. aquaticus rpsT, and this complementation restored wild-type levels of growth.
source: We found that rpsT is essential in T. thermophilus, but that its loss could be complemented by wild-type and mutant T. aquaticus rpsT, and that this complementation restored wild-type levels of growth (Figure 8e).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental growth curve results and references Figure 8e.

claim: When the selection pressure from kanamycin was removed, no reversal in the PCR products was detected for any strain.
source: Moreover, when the selection pressure from kanamycin was removed, no reversal in the PCR products was detected for any strain (Figure 8c and d, panel 3), which conﬁrms that chromosomal rpsT was substantially displaced during kanamycin treatment.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental PCR screening results after removal of selection pressure.

claim: rpsT from T. aquaticus and its two mutated alleles are neutral with respect to survival and growth for T. thermophilus.
source: We conclude that rpsT from T. aquaticus and its two mutated alleles are neutral with respect to survival and growth for T. thermophilus.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the complementation and growth experiments.

claim: The mutations introduced into RPS20 do not affect negatively the interaction between RPS20 and its cognate RNA.
source: This demonstrates that the mutations we introduced do not affect negatively the interaction between RPS20 and its cognate RNA, and that therefore such mutations could have been sampled multiply and in a cumulative fashion by neutral drift during the course of evolution.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vivo complementation experiments showing neutral effects.

claim: The mutations introduced into RPS20 could have been sampled multiply and in a cumulative fashion by neutral drift during the course of evolution.
source: This demonstrates that the mutations we introduced do not affect negatively the interaction between RPS20 and its cognate RNA, and that therefore such mutations could have been sampled multiply and in a cumulative fashion by neutral drift during the course of evolution.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about evolutionary processes based on the neutrality of the mutations.

claim: In E. coli and Salmonella enterica, rpsT has been reported to be non-essential, but its deletion significantly lowers growth rates.
source: In E. coli and Salmonella enterica, rpsT has been reported to be non-essential, but its deletion significantly lowers growth rates (Bubunenko et al., 2007; Tobin et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites two studies reporting the effects of rpsT deletion in other organisms.

claim: The overwhelming majority of random polypeptides do not appear to have a folded structure.
source: Despite the widespread problems to reach and maintain the folded state, natural proteins nevertheless form a best-case group, since the overwhelming majority of random polypeptides do not appear to have a folded structure (Keefe and Szostak, 2001; Wei et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript cites two studies supporting this observation about random polypeptides.

claim: 40 peptides have been described whose conservation in diverse folds suggests that they predated folded proteins.
source: We have recently described 40 such peptides whose conservation in diverse folds suggests that they predated folded proteins (Alva et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites Alva et al., 2015 for this previous work.

claim: Core ribosomal proteins close to the catalytic center almost entirely lack secondary structure.
source: Thus, core ribosomal proteins offer a window into the time when proteins were acquiring the ability to fold. Those close to the catalytic center almost entirely lack secondary structure.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about ribosomal protein structure in relation to their position.

claim: Further away from the ribosomal catalytic center, the secondary structure content of ribosomal proteins gradually increases.
source: Further away from the center, their secondary structure content gradually increases and at the periphery, these secondary structure elements become arranged into topologies that parallel those seen in cytosolic proteins (Hsiao et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites Hsiao et al., 2009 for this observation about ribosomal protein structure.

claim: The structures of ribosomal proteins chart a path of progressive emancipation from the RNA scaffold.
source: Collectively, the structures of ribosomal proteins chart a path of progressive emancipation from the RNA scaffold.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural observations about ribosomal proteins.

claim: Peripheral ribosomal proteins still mostly assume their structure only in the context of the ribosomal RNA.
source: Even the peripheral proteins, however, still mostly assume their structure only in the context of the ribosomal RNA, as exemplified by RPS20 in our study (Supplementary file 1F, see also Paterakis et al., 1983).
evidence: The manuscript cites experimental data and Paterakis et al., 1983 to support this observation.

claim: Simple repetition of the RPS20 hairpin was not sufficient to form a folded structure, but the repeat protein was so close to a folded structure that only two point mutations per repeat were necessary to allow it to fold reliably.
source: Simple repetition was not sufficient in our case, but the repeat protein was so close to a folded structure that only two point mutations per repeat were necessary to allow it to fold reliably.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results from the design and characterization of M2.

claim: All present-day TPR domains whose function has been characterized mediate protein-protein interactions by binding to linear sequence motifs in unstructured polypeptide segments.
source: All present-day TPR domains whose function has been characterized mediate protein-protein interactions by binding to linear sequence motifs in unstructured polypeptide segments (D'Andrea and Regan, 2003; Zeytuni and Zarivach, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites two reviews summarizing the functional characterization of TPR domains.

claim: TPRpred was used with TPR profile tpr2.8 to identify TPR unit-like sequences from all protein sequences of known structures in the PDB.
source: First, TPRpred program with TPR proﬁle tpr2.8 was used to identify TPR unit like sequences from all protein sequences of known structures in the Protein Data Bank (PDB, RRID:SCR_012820) (Berman et al., 2000).
evidence: The manuscript describes the computational method used.

claim: 68,197 non-identical protein sequences from the PDB were scanned by TPRpred with default parameters.
source: In total, 68,197 sequences were scanned by using TPRpred with default parameters.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of sequences analyzed.

claim: 646 hits were retained from the TPRpred scan using a p-value cutoff of 1.0e−4.
source: Only fragments predicted to be TPR with a p-value lower than 1.0e−4 were retained (646 hits).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of hits from the computational analysis.

claim: The false discovery rate associated with the p-value cutoff of 1.0e−4 was estimated to be 1.0 ± 0.4%.
source: We estimated the false discovery rate (FDR) (Noble, 2009) associated with this p-value cutoff using a simulated sequence dataset generated by using the amino-acid composition derived from the PDB sequences. The dataset contains the same number of sequences of the same length distribution as the PDB sequences. The FDR was estimated to be the ratio of the number of hits in the simulated dataset to the number of detected hits in the PDB sequences (Noble, 2009). We repeated the simulation 100 times and the FDR was estimated to be 1.0 ± 0.4%.
evidence: The manuscript describes the FDR estimation method and reports the result.

claim: The highest correlation in TPR sequences occurs between positions 7 and 23, with the most commonly observed combinations being R7-D23 and L7-Y23.
source: The results of both approaches revealed that the highest correlation occurs between positions 7 and 23 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), with the most commonly observed combinations being R7-D23 and L7-Y23.
evidence: The manuscript reports results from direct coupling analysis and mutual information analysis, referencing Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: CTPR3 structure (PDB id: 1na0, chain A) was taken as the main template to build an initial TPR structure model using RPS20-hhta.
source: CTPR3 structure of an idealized TPR repeat (Main et al., 2003b) (PDB id: 1na0, chain A) was taken as the main template to build an initial TPR structure model using RPS20-hhta.
evidence: The manuscript describes the structural modeling approach.

claim: The structure of RPS20 from Thermus thermophilus HB8 (PDB id: 2vqe, chain T) was used as the structure template for the last repeat and the stop helix because it was the structure with the best resolution (2.5 Å).
source: The structure of RPS20 from Thermus thermophilus HB8 (PDB id: 2vqe, chain T) was used because it was the structure with the best resolution (2.5 Å).
evidence: The manuscript describes the rationale for template selection.

claim: Rosetta programs fixbb and relax were used to model the designed TPR sequences and refine the structures.
source: We then modeled the designed TPR sequences using RPS20-hhta onto the hybrid structure template using Rosetta programs fixbb and relax (Das and Baker, 2008).
evidence: The manuscript describes the computational modeling method and cites the Rosetta reference.

claim: Rosetta 3.4 was used for the in silico structure modeling and refinement.
source: Rosetta 3.4 was used in the work.
evidence: The manuscript specifies the version of software used.
